crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Credit Scoring with Alternative Data
children.blurb: Credit scoring with alternative data covers the use of nontraditional records, such as rent, utility, telecom, cash flow, and public records, to estimate repayment risk when traditional bureau files are thin or stale.

children.name: Covenant Extraction
children.blurb: Covenant extraction is the work of turning the terms of credit agreements, indentures, and loan documents into structured data that a credit team can query and monitor.

children.name: Predicting Distress and Default
children.blurb: Predicting distress and default covers the estimation of a borrower's or issuer's likelihood of failing to meet debt obligations over horizons set by the portfolio or regulatory context.

children.name: Modelling the Yield Curve
children.blurb: Modelling the yield curve covers the estimation of the term structure of interest rates from market prices, including spot rates, forward rates, discount factors and par yields.

children.name: Stress Testing Structured Credit
children.blurb: Stress testing structured credit covers securitized products such as RMBS, CMBS, ABS, CLOs and CDOs, and the tranches that sit on top of underlying pools.

sections.body: Fixed income and credit risk is the work of deciding who will pay back a loan, when they will pay it, and what happens when they do not. In practice, artificial intelligence is being used to read loan documents, score borrowers who have thin credit files, flag early signs of trouble in a company, and run large simulations of losses across pools of mortgages and corporate debt. Models now parse covenant language in credit agreements, pull signals from payment and transaction records, and estimate default probabilities from a mix of financial and behavioural data. The work is less about replacing analysts than about compressing the time it takes to read, sort and stress a portfolio, and about finding patterns across thousands of borrowers that a single reviewer could never hold in mind. The output still feeds a human decision about pricing, holding or hedging a position.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this field are mature. Credit scoring with conventional data has been statistical for decades, and machine learning mainly improves the edges, especially for borrowers with little history. Covenant extraction has moved from keyword search to language models that can identify definitions, baskets and carve-outs, though accuracy falls on poorly scanned or heavily negotiated documents. Distress prediction is genuinely hard because defaults are rare, labels arrive late, and a model that fits the past can miss a new kind of shock. Yield curve modelling is a smaller, more settled problem, but the curve is a market price, not a prediction, and no model removes that. Stress testing structured credit remains the least settled area, because the underlying cash flows are complex, data is sparse, and the honest limit is that a simulation is only as good as its assumptions about correlation and recovery.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here form a chain from the individual borrower up to the whole portfolio. Credit Scoring with Alternative Data is the entry point, covering how non traditional signals are used to judge a single borrower, and it sets up the data questions that run through everything else. Covenant Extraction sits beside it on the legal side, showing how models read the terms that constrain a borrower once a loan exists. Predicting Distress and Default takes those signals and asks how early trouble can be seen, which is where the hardest statistical problems live. Modelling the Yield Curve steps back to the price of money over time, the backdrop against which every credit is valued. Stress Testing Structured Credit is the widest page, pulling scoring, covenants, default and rates into scenarios for pools of debt, and a reader would go there last to see how the pieces combine under pressure.
